newsitem.title: USA: Louisiana dazed by Danny's surprising punch.
newsitem.headline: Louisiana dazed by Danny's surprising punch.

text.p: Coastal Louisiana residents, dazed by a surprisingly powerful punch from Hurricane Danny, began assessing damage on Friday as the Gulf Coast braced for round two with the storm.

Danny, a minimal hurricane, swept across the tip of Louisiana early on Friday, flooding highways and flattening power lines with winds gusting up to 100 miles an hour, authorities said. No deaths or serious injuries were reported.

By 9 a.m. CDT (10 a.m. EDT) (1400 GMT), an estimated 10,000 homes and businesses in the sparsely populated area along the Louisiana coast were without electricity as wind and rain began lashing lower St. Bernard Parish east of New Orleans.

A National Weather Service spokesman in Slidell, La., said there was no confirmation of tornadoes spawned by the slow-moving storm in Louisiana, but tornado warnings were posted along the storm's leading edge as far east as the Florida panhandle.

Hurricane warning flags were raised from Morgan City, La., east to Destin, Fla., as the storm swept across the southern tip of Louisiana and moved back into the Gulf of Mexico's Breton Sound wildlife area.
Mississippi Gov. Kirk Fordice issued a state of emergency but civil defence officials in coastal communities said the main force of the storm was expected to remain offshore.
In Biloxi, Miss., Police Chief Tommy Moffett said authorities were considering opening a shelter for a large number of stranded tourists at area beaches and casinos.

"Right now, it's just a matter of trying to get ready while we wait to see if there really is anything to get ready for," he said. "We know that with hurricanes, you just never know what's going to happen. Danny could come here, head east, or turn around and go back to Louisiana."

The Copa casino in Gulfport, Miss., one of 11 floating casinos operating along the Gulf Coast, was closed for a second day on Friday but state officials decided not to order the remaining barge casinos shuttered ahead of the storm.

"It's a very difficult process to close the casinos. You have to offload and secure all of the paper money and then lock the chips and coins into vaults. They're too heavy to move so they use them for ballast," said Warren Strain, spokesman with the Mississippi Gaming Commission.

No mandatory evacuations have been ordered in Mississippi, but boat owners were moving vessels into protected harbours and windows were being boarded up and taped as Mississippi Gulf Coast residents braced for Danny's expected arrival Saturday.
"The latest forecast puts landfall between Gulfport (Miss.) and Mobile (Ala.), probably early tomorrow morning," Jill Hasling, a forecaster with private forecaster Weather Research Centre said.

Alabama officials issued a nonmandatory evacuation order for southern Baldwin and Mobile counties along the coast, and opened six shelters further inland to prepare for possible flooding from up to 20 inches of rainfall from the storm.

In Louisiana, Lower Plaquemines Parish, southeast of New Orleans, took the brunt of the storm early Friday as the eye of the slow-moving hurricane drifted back into the Gulf of Mexico, dumping up to 10 inches of rain on the area.
Plaquemines officials closed the only highway running the length of the parish Friday morning as high water made driving extremely dangerous, a sheriff's deputy said.
"We don't have any injuries reported, and so far, thank God, no major property damage, but I really don't have time to talk," he said.

West of Plaquemines, officials in Grand Isle, Louisiana's only inhabited barrier island, reported heavy damage and erosion. Most of the island's 1,530 residents obeyed a mandatory evacuation order Thursday and moved inland.
Grand Isle Mayor Pro Tem Ray Santini told Reuters the island was severely flooded and officials did not know when residents would be allowed to return.
In New Orleans, the storm's impact was limited to occasional showers and wind gusts as the city was spared the heavy rains that could have caused widespread flooding.
Late-night revellers on Bourbon Street barely broke stride as light rains and intermittent gusts swept the historic French Quarter as Danny hit New Orleans with a weak punch.

The storm first made landfall overnight between Grand Isle and the mouth of the Mississippi River, and the eye of the hurricane at 10 a.m. CDT (1500 GMT) was located about 90 miles southwest of Mobile, Ala., near latitude 29.7 north, longitude 89.2 west and moving northeast at 5 miles an hour.
Hurricane force winds of 75 miles an hour extended outward about 25 miles from the centre, with the strongest gusts on the east side of the slow-moving storm.
